title: The fig tree and the temple (Mark 11:12–19)
hookLine: Mark sandwiches a barren fig tree around the temple scene: a house of prayer for all nations
carry: a house of prayer for all
last: THE LORD HAS NEED OF IT.

cards: The next morning, walking in from Bethany, Jesus is hungry. Far off he spots a fig tree in full leaf and goes to look for fruit. Nothing but leaves.
Then Mark adds a line readers keep tripping over: "for the time of figs was not yet." It wasn't even the season. And Jesus speaks to the tree: no one will ever eat fruit from you again.
His disciples heard it, Mark says. Fruit out of season? Hold on to that puzzle.
Mark likes to make sandwiches: he starts one story, cuts into the middle with another, then finishes the first. The fig tree is the bread. Here comes the filling.

teach.b: They come into Jerusalem, and Jesus goes into the temple courts and throws out the buyers and the sellers. He overturns the tables of the money changers and the seats of the people selling doves.
In the Law of Moses, doves were the offering for someone who couldn't afford a lamb. He won't let anyone carry goods through the temple, as if it were a shortcut. He quotes two old prophets.
In the King James Bible: "Is it not written, My house shall be called of all nations the house of prayer? but ye have made it a den of thieves."
The first half is Isaiah: a house of prayer for all nations, foreigners included. Matthew and Luke, telling the same scene, leave out of all nations; Mark keeps it.
Some readers think the trading filled the outer court, where people who weren't Jewish could come to pray.
The second half is Jeremiah. A den of thieves isn't where robbers rob. It's the hideout they run back to, to feel safe.

Jesus stands where Israel's prophets stood, speaking from inside his own tradition about his own temple. The chief priests and scribes hear, and start looking for a way to destroy him, because the crowds are spellbound.
Some readers see the fig tree as a sign acted out, a picture of the temple scene: plenty of leaves, lots of activity, and no fruit.

teach.h: MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED OF ALL NATIONS THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.
teach.b: Mark doesn't explain; he sets them side by side.

how: Some churches pray for the nations of the world in their weekly prayers, and the temple scene is often read during Holy Week, remembering Jesus's words that God's house is for all people.

games.q: you walk into the temple courts in Jerusalem. tables of coins, cages of doves, people cutting through with goods. what does Jesus do?
o: find a quiet corner to pray.
pay the temple tax and leave.
games.why: he overturns the tables and the dove-sellers' seats, and quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah: a house of prayer for all nations.

practice: Picture a map of the world and travel slowly across it: your own town, your country, a place in the news this week, a place you've never thought about at all. Imagine all of them welcome in one house of prayer.
If you pray, pray for the nations one place at a time, by name; if you don't, simply wish each place well as you pass over it.

wordCard.voice: Isaiah, the prophet whose words Jesus quotes: my house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations.

orig.note: Greek: a cave, a den. in Mark 11:17, a cave of robbers, echoing Jeremiah 7:11.

carryVoice: Your line: a house of prayer for all. Of all nations, Mark says, foreigners included. See you tomorrow.
